mechanism_name: fstab-level dm-verity independent of AVB metadata
how_it_works: Android's fs_mgr supports two independent, mutually-exclusive ways to turn on dm-verity for a given fstab line, selected purely by which fs_mgr flag word appears in that line's flags column: the legacy 'verify' flag (vboot 1.0, pre-AVB) and the 'avb' flag (vboot 2.0 / Android Verified Boot). They do not share a code path. When fs_mgr sees 'avb' on a partition's fstab entry, it calls into libavb's avb_slot_verify(), which reads the vbmeta struct's AVB_VBMETA_FLAGS (flags=2 = verification disabled) and, when disabled, skips constructing any verity table for that partition -- this is the path already ruled out by the confirmed vbmeta flags=2/algorithm_type=0 finding. When fs_mgr instead sees the older 'verify' flag on a line, it never touches vbmeta at all: first-stage init reads verity metadata (a signed table of block hashes plus algorithm/salt info) that is appended directly after the filesystem's data on that same block device (or, on some OEM builds, held in a side-car metadata partition), verifies its RSA signature against a key baked into the boot ramdisk/init binary (traditionally /verity_key), and if that checks out builds the dm-verity device-mapper table straight from that metadata -- entirely independent of AVB/vbmeta. On this device the compiled fstab is reached either as a plaintext fstab.<hardware> file inside the boot.img ramdisk (first-stage init explicitly does 'compiled-in fstab mounting' before switch_root, per the task's own device facts) or as a device-tree 'firmware/android/fstab' node with a per-partition 'fsmgr_flags' string property; either location can carry 'verify' on the /system (or '/') line without AVB being involved anywhere. If that were the case here, editing files inside the ext4 image via a recovery loop-mount (which never goes through fs_mgr/dm-verity at all -- it's a raw block-device write) would leave the filesystem bytes changed but the previously-computed verity hash tree stale, so the *next real boot's* dm-verity target would recompute per-block hashes over the now-modified region and find a mismatch against the old hash tree.
fits_observed_symptoms: (1) Write succeeds pre-reboot: fits -- loop-mounting the raw ext4 image from recovery bypasses fs_mgr/dm-verity entirely, so nothing there would block the write. (2) Survives unmount/remount within the same recovery session: fits -- no verity device-mapper target is active in this recovery flow at all, so nothing re-checks the hash tree until a real boot invokes fs_mgr. (3) Reverts only after a real power-cycle boot: fits *directionally* (dm-verity is only evaluated by first/second-stage init during an actual boot, never during a recovery loop-mount), but the mechanism explains the *timing* far better than the *content*. Per source.android.com's own dm-verity documentation, a hash mismatch does not cause the kernel to substitute or restore prior good content -- there is no backing store of the original bytes anywhere in the verity metadata, only hashes. Depending on androidboot.veritymode, the kernel instead returns an I/O error on the offending block (default/eio mode), reboots the device (restart/enforcing mode with restart_on_corruption), or -- in logging mode -- passes the read through while merely logging a corruption warning, which would still surface the *actual modified* bytes to the reader, not a silent reversion to the old ones. None of the four documented dm-verity failure modes (eio, restart, panic, logging) produce a clean, error-free, exact reversion to prior content, so as literally described ('init.rc itself reverts to original content' with no boot failure or error mentioned) this is a POOR fit on the content-substitution axis, even though it is a good fit on the boot-only-timing axis. (4) boot_completed marker never appears in /cache: only weakly consistent -- if dm-verity actually failed the /system mount outright (EIO on the modified block, which likely includes the init.rc block or metadata near it), second-stage init could not switch_root into /system at all, which should manifest as a visible boot failure/bootloop rather than a device that quietly finishes booting with the old init.rc content, which the task's framing implies is happening repeatedly and cleanly. This is a moderate contradiction unless the modified byte range happens to fall in a *different* dm-verity block than the one actually read at boot (unlikely for a same-file edit) or unless the device is in logging mode and something else entirely (not dm-verity) is responsible for restoring the old bytes. (5) AVB confirmed disabled: fits as the precondition that makes this AVB-independent path worth considering at all. (6) ext4 not squashfs: neutral -- dm-verity operates block-wise beneath the filesystem and works the same over ext4 as over any other fs. (7) non-A/B: neutral/fits -- the legacy 'verify' flag predates A/B slotting and has no dependency on slot mechanics, so device being non-A/B is not disqualifying, though it does make the coexistence with dynamic/logical partitions (super, offset 1048576, size 800915456) somewhat unusual (see known_precedent).
known_precedent: The 'verify' (vboot 1.0) vs 'avb' (vboot 2.0) split is real and documented on source.android.com's dm-verity and verified-boot pages, and was the standard mechanism on Android devices roughly Android 4.4 through early Nougat before AVB became the norm. The XDA/root community's well-known 'Universal DM-Verity, ForceEncrypt, Disk Quota Disabler' scripts work precisely by stripping the 'verify' (and 'forceencrypt') fs_mgr flag word out of a device's ramdisk fstab, confirming this is a common, real, independently-triggerable path distinct from AVB/vbmeta patching. [uncertain] No public documentation was found of a shipping Rockchip RK3326 Android-Go STB (or this TXCZ box specifically) combining the legacy 'verify' flag with dynamic partitions (logical /system inside super) -- these are normally features of different Android generations (legacy verify predates dynamic partitions; Google's dynamic-partition tooling assumes AVB hashtree descriptors for logical partitions), so an OEM shipping both together would be an unusual, non-standard build rather than a documented reference configuration. This device's specific fstab has not yet been inspected to confirm 'verify' is actually present.
likelihood: Low. The mechanism is real and AOSP-standard, and its boot-only timing matches the symptom, but its actual failure behavior (I/O error, device restart, or logged-passthrough of the *real* modified data) does not produce the specific silent, error-free, exact reversion to old content that was observed, and combining legacy non-AVB verity with a dynamic/logical /system partition would itself be a non-standard OEM configuration that hasn't been confirmed to exist on this device.
test_procedure: All steps below are read-only and run from the already-working recovery adb root shell; step 6 requires one real reboot cycle (which the task says is already being done to reproduce the bug) but does not require any new access. 1) Inspect the fstab shipped inside the already loop-mounted /system image directly for the fs_mgr flags word on the /system (or '/') line: `adb shell find <system_mount_path> -maxdepth 4 -iname 'fstab*' -exec cat {} \;` and look for 'verify' vs 'avb' in the flags column. 2) Check the device-tree-embedded fstab, which the kernel exposes regardless of recovery vs normal boot since it comes from the boot/dtbo partition handed off by the bootloader: `adb shell find /proc/device-tree/firmware/android -maxdepth 3` then `adb shell cat /proc/device-tree/firmware/android/fstab/system/fsmgr_flags` and `.../dev`. 3) Extract boot.img's first-stage ramdisk and check for a plaintext fstab.<hardware> file (the task confirms this ramdisk has no init.rc, but doesn't rule out an fstab file coexisting with the compiled-in mount step): `adb pull /dev/block/by-name/boot boot.img`, then on a host machine `unpack_bootimg --boot_img boot.img --out out_boot`, extract the ramdisk cpio (`cpio -idv < out_boot/ramdisk`), and `grep -R -E 'verify|avb' fstab.*`. 4) Re-check the full kernel cmdline for verity-mode hints already partially read for the selinux=permissive finding: `adb shell cat /proc/cmdline | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -iE 'verity|avb'`. 5) Check whether the system partition itself carries its own appended legacy-verity metadata block or a standalone AVB footer independent of the vbmeta partition (a footer-based AVB config would also be independent of the already-checked vbmeta partition and is worth ruling out at the same time): dump the tail of the /system logical partition/loop device and scan for the 'AVBf' magic or verity metadata magic near its declared end (offset 1048576 + size 800915456): `adb shell tail -c 8192 <system_block_or_loop_device> | xxd | grep -iE 'avbf|verity'`; if avbtool is available on a pulled copy of the image, `avbtool info_image --image system.img` gives a definitive answer. 6) The fully conclusive dynamic check, which matches the task's own observation that the revert only manifests after a real boot: immediately after the next reproduction reboot, race to capture state before/while the revert would be occurring: `adb wait-for-device && adb root && adb shell 'dmesg | grep -iE "verity|corrupt|EIO|dm-"'`, `adb shell dmsetup ls` and `adb shell dmsetup table` (look for a target of type 'verity' mapping the /system block device), and `adb shell cat /proc/mounts | grep -E ' / | /system '`. Presence of a verity dm target plus corruption/EIO log lines confirms this mechanism; a total absence of any verity target in dmsetup output rules it out entirely.
bypass_or_fix: Only apply if step 1-6 above actually locate a 'verify' flag or standalone verity/AVB-footer metadata for /system; do not preemptively patch anything. If a plaintext fstab in the boot ramdisk carries 'verify' (found in step 3): unpack boot.img's ramdisk, remove the 'verify' flag word (and any 'verify_key_path=...' companion flag) from the /system line only, repack the ramdisk (cpio) and rebuild boot.img with the original kernel/cmdline/pagesize/header version via `mkbootimg`, then flash the rebuilt image to the boot partition -- this is the same technique used by the well-known XDA 'Universal DM-Verity/ForceEncrypt Disabler' scripts. If the fstab lives in a device-tree overlay instead (found in step 2 pointing to a dtbo-sourced node rather than a ramdisk file): decompile the relevant dtb/dtbo (`mkdtimg`/`dtc`), remove 'verify' from the 'fsmgr_flags' property under firmware/android/fstab/system, recompile and reflash that dtbo/boot image. If instead a legacy verity metadata block (or an independent AVB footer) is found appended directly on the system partition itself rather than gated by an fstab flag (found in step 5): zero out or truncate that trailing metadata region on the raw block device so fs_mgr/first-stage-init finds no verity magic at boot and silently falls back to an unverified mount, e.g. `dd if=/dev/zero of=<system_block_device> seek=<metadata_offset> bs=1 count=64`. Whichever image is patched (boot.img or a dtbo), confirm the bootloader does not itself separately signature-check that image before accepting it -- if it does, this fix alone will not persist and the bootloader-level check must be addressed first.
risk_level: Read-only diagnostic (steps 1-6): low risk, no writes, uses only adb pull/cat/find/dmesg/dmsetup against partitions and proc/device-tree nodes already established as accessible. Bypass/fix steps: moderate risk -- they involve rebuilding and reflashing a boot.img or dtbo, which if malformed (wrong header version, wrong page size, wrong cmdline) can produce a device that fails to boot at all; always keep the original pulled boot.img/dtbo as a known-good backup before flashing a patched one, and confirm recovery access remains available as a fallback.
